notes: CITB levy appeal on automated off-site joinery; tribunal finding on paragraph 2(xx) Scope Order upheld on narrow grounds.

enrichment.short_title: CITB levy appeal: automated off-site joinery exclusion
key_facts: The Construction Industry Training Board appealed against an Employment Tribunal decision setting aside a levy of about £2,000 on Scalegold Joinery Ltd.
Scalegold produced bespoke wooden joinery off-site using computer-controlled machinery and skilled craftsmen, including items later installed in buildings.
The tribunal held that paragraph 2(c)(xx) of the Scope Order excluded automated off-site manufacture of building products from timber.
CITB argued there was no conflict between paragraph 1(c) and the exception, and that use of power tools did not make the activity automated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Administrative Court on a point of law from an Employment Appeal Tribunal decision on an industrial training levy assessment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the tribunal could fairly be read as finding the activity was automated, saving the decision on that narrow ground; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 2(c)(xx) is an exception to paragraph 1(c) rather than a conflicting provision; automated activity means production by machines rather than craftsmen using machine tools; a tribunal decision may be upheld if, read fairly, it contains sufficient material findings even if reasoning is inelegant.
legal_issues: Whether Scalegold's joinery business fell within the construction industry for levy purposes
Meaning of 'automated' in paragraph 2(c)(xx) of the Scope Order
Relationship between paragraph 1(c)(ii) and paragraph 2(c)(xx)
Whether off-site manufacture is excluded only if another person installs the products
linked_authorities: Mark Wilkinson Furniture Ltd v CITB

confidence.notes: Outcome, statutory framework and interpretation of automation are clearly stated. Permission refusal and narrow basis of decision are explicit.

notes: White v Jones inter vivos trust negligence; strike-out refusal in developing area of law upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Trust beneficiaries' negligence claim against accountant
key_facts: Colin Richards, a chartered accountant, advised David and Alison Hughes to set up the offshore Thedis Trust for their children's education using royalty payments from a share sale.
The trust and Swiss trading company Cedrus AG absorbed most funds in fees and taxes; the children received no benefit.
The children sued Richards in tort alleging negligence in the investment and monitoring retainers; the parents brought a parallel claim.
Richards applied to strike out the children's claim, arguing only the parents had a remedy under White v Jones principles.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal to strike out or dismiss the children's negligence claim at a preliminary stage under CPR Part 3.4/24.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the children's claim was allowed to proceed to trial alongside the parents' claim.
enrichment.ratio: In an uncertain and developing area at the contract-tort interface, a claim should not be struck out unless it is certain to fail; obiter remarks in White v Jones on inter vivos gifts do not determinatively exclude beneficiary claims where effective transactions divested the settlors and loss emerged years later.
legal_issues: Whether intended trust beneficiaries may sue a negligent professional adviser in tort
Application of White v Jones to inter vivos trust arrangements
Whether the monitoring retainer gives rise to a distinct duty to beneficiaries
Appropriate use of strike-out in developing negligence law

notes: CCRC-referred 1971 murder appeal; Lucas lies direction challenge and plastic strip summing-up grounds rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Bain murder appeal: lies direction and summing-up
key_facts: Alfred Nathan Bain was convicted in 1971 of murdering prostitute Mary McCormack by strangulation with plastic from his loudspeaker.
The prosecution case rested on alibi lies, timing of his movements, and his conduct after discovering the body.
The CCRC referred the case because of alleged inadequacy of the trial judge's directions on lies told by the defendant.
Bain died in 2001; his daughter pursued the appeal with leave under section 44A.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Reference by the Criminal Cases Review Commission; full rehearing of appeal grounds including lies directions and summing-up on plastic strip evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction held safe despite deficiencies judged by modern Lucas standards; additional summing-up grounds also rejected.
enrichment.ratio: A summing-up that endorsed defence counsel's explanation that lies may be told for innocent reasons and conditioned reliance on lies on Crown evidence being accepted satisfied Broadhurst principles for a 1971 trial; alleged unfairness over loudspeaker plastic strip evidence was not established.
legal_issues: Whether the trial judge adequately directed the jury on lies by the defendant
Application of R v Lucas and R v Burge & Pegg standards to a 1971 conviction
Whether summing-up on access to the plastic strip was unfair
Safety of conviction where alibi and post-discovery lies were central
linked_authorities: Broadhurst v R [1963] AC 441
R v Lucas (1981) 73 Cr App R 159
R v Burge & Pegg [1996] 1 Cr App R 163
R v Ritchens (1994) 98 Cr App R 43
R v Robinson [1996] Crim LR 417
R v Bentley [2002] 1 Cr App R 305

confidence.notes: Detailed treatment of lies directions and outcome is clear. Transcript of summing-up was incomplete but court had first appeal judgment.

notes: Turner irregular chambers indication; oral evidence in Court of Appeal found guilty pleas were free choices.

enrichment.short_title: Nazham fraud pleas: irregular judicial indication
key_facts: Hameed and Murtaza Nazham pleaded guilty on re-arraignment to conspiracy to defraud banks using false identities over about seven years.
Before trial Judge Coates indicated in chambers that a guilty plea would attract a sentence of under four years.
Both were sentenced to three and a half years and substantial confiscation orders followed.
On appeal they contended the chambers discussion improperly fettered their freedom to choose their plea.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave on irregular pre-trial discussions in the judge's chambers; Court of Appeal heard oral evidence from appellants and trial counsel.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; irregular judicial indication did not deprive either appellant of a free choice to plead guilty.
enrichment.ratio: An irregular Turner-type indication in chambers does not automatically render a subsequent guilty plea a nullity; the court must examine what was relayed to the defendant and whether improper pressure caused the change of plea, and may prefer counsel's evidence to the appellant's.
legal_issues: Whether chambers discussions before a change of plea were irregular under Turner
Whether irregularity rendered guilty pleas nullities
Whether freedom of choice was impaired by judicial sentence indication
Appropriateness of receiving oral evidence on appeal
linked_authorities: Hall [1968] 52 Cr App R 528
Turner [1970] 54 Cr App R 352
Brook [1970] CLR 600
Inns [1974] 60 Cr App R 231
Llewellyn [1978] 67 Cr App R 149
Pitman [1991] 1 All ER 468
Attorney General's Reference No 44 of 2000 (Robin Peverett) [2001] 1 Cr App R 416
Pitts [2001] EWCA Crim 846

confidence.notes: Court heard extensive evidence and gave detailed reasons. Irregularity of chambers discussion was conceded; causation issue was central.

notes: SIAC bail interim decision for certified terrorist detainee; jurisdiction and Article 6 issues adjourned.

enrichment.short_title: SIAC bail for certified terrorist detainee G
key_facts: G, an Algerian certified as a suspected international terrorist under ATCSA, had been detained since December 2001.
SIAC dismissed his certification appeal in October 2003 but in principle granted bail in January 2004 on strict house arrest conditions due to deteriorating mental health.
The Secretary of State challenged SIAC's jurisdiction to grant bail when not seized of a pending appeal and the Court of Appeal's jurisdiction under section 7 SIACA.
G argued that denying bail would breach Articles 3, 6 and 8 of the ECHR.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interim decision on permission to appeal from SIAC's in-principle bail decision; application restored for further argument on jurisdiction and incompatibility.
enrichment.outcome: Interim decision: section 7 SIACA held not to confer jurisdiction over the bail decision; matter restored for further argument on SIAC jurisdiction, possible judicial review, and ATCSA compatibility.
enrichment.ratio: A post-determination bail application under section 24 ATCSA is not a 'final determination of an appeal' within section 7 SIACA, so the Court of Appeal has no statutory appeal jurisdiction; difficult questions remain whether SIAC may grant indefinite bail and whether exclusion of review breaches Article 6.
legal_issues: Whether SIAC had jurisdiction to grant bail after dismissing G's certification appeal
Whether section 7 SIACA covers appeals against bail decisions
Whether ATCSA is incompatible with the ECHR if bail review is unavailable
Whether judicial review lies against SIAC bail decisions
linked_authorities: Secretary of State for the Home Department v Rehman [2003] 1 AC 153
Taylor v Lawrence [2002] EWCA Civ 90
Anisminic v Foreign Compensation Commission [1969] 2 AC 147
In re Racal Communications Ltd [1981] AC 375
Reg v Manchester Crown Court ex parte DPP [1993] 1 WLR 1524

confidence.notes: Interim procedural ruling only; merits of bail and final jurisdiction questions expressly reserved. Pill LJ dissented on section 7.

notes: Takeaway robbery wounding; self-defence misdirection quashed conviction and section 20 substituted.

enrichment.short_title: Takeaway robbery: self-defence misdirection and substituted conviction
key_facts: Mark O'Sullivan pleaded guilty to attempted robbery at a fried chicken shop while drunk and armed with a kitchen knife.
Yogesh, a staff member, was stabbed in the arm and stomach; the prosecution alleged intentional section 18 wounding, the defence case was accidental injury during a melee.
The judge directed the jury that self-defence was the defendant's primary case rather than lack of intent.
The judge also made inappropriate remarks including calling part of the defendant's evidence 'arrant rubbish' and saying he probably did not deserve a fair trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction on section 18 wounding with intent following a Crown Court trial at St Albans.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; section 18 conviction quashed as unsafe; section 20 wounding conviction substituted with three years concurrent.
enrichment.ratio: Where the defendant's real defence at trial was accidental wounding without intent, presenting self-defence as the primary issue and framing lack of intent as a fallback misdirected the jury and deprived the defendant of a fair trial on the central question of intent.
legal_issues: Whether the judge misdirected the jury by treating self-defence as the primary defence
Whether accident/lack of intent was properly left to the jury
Effect of section 34 direction based on mischaracterised defence
Whether judge's comments gave appearance of bias
linked_authorities: R v Iroegbu

confidence.notes: Court's reasoning on misdirection and substituted section 20 conviction is explicit. Bias grounds were not determinative.

notes: Drug trafficking confiscation; 25% section 4(4)(b) deductions held lawful partial injustice avoidance.

enrichment.short_title: Drug trafficking confiscation: partial section 4 assumptions
key_facts: Deprince was convicted of fraudulent evasion of cocaine importation at Gatwick and sentenced to 14 years.
At confiscation the judge found benefit of £149,433 and realisable assets of £125,369.
For five income and expenditure items the judge applied 25% deductions after finding serious risk of injustice under section 4(4)(b) if full assumptions were made.
The appellant argued that once injustice risk was found, no assumption could be made for that property or expenditure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave against confiscation order on construction of section 4(4) Drug Trafficking Act 1994.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; partial percentage reductions to eliminate serious risk of injustice were held lawful.
enrichment.ratio: Section 4(4) permits consideration of part of a particular property or expenditure item; where a judge finds serious risk of injustice if full assumptions are made, a generous percentage discount may lawfully eliminate that risk without treating the entire item as excluded from assumptions.
legal_issues: Whether section 4(4)(b) prohibits any assumption once serious injustice risk is identified
Whether partial percentage reductions are permitted under section 4(4)
Meaning of 'any particular property or expenditure'
Proper approach to avoiding injustice in confiscation proceedings
linked_authorities: R v Rezvi [2002] 1 All ER 801
R v Benjafield [2002] 1 All ER 815

confidence.notes: Statutory construction issue and five challenged findings are clearly analysed. Judge's 25% figure was not precisely explained but approach upheld.

notes: Majority conviction on one indecent assault count; inconsistent verdict challenge rejected under R v G.

enrichment.short_title: Rogers: inconsistent verdicts on indecent assault counts
key_facts: Rogers was tried on four rape and two indecent assault counts relating to three teenage girls.
Rape counts were withdrawn for insufficient evidence of lack of consent; jury acquitted on all but one indecent assault count concerning complainant S's first incident.
The prosecution alleged Rogers groomed a vulnerable bereaved family to obtain sexual access; he denied any sexual contact.
The judge directed the jury to consider each count separately.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave against majority conviction on one count of indecent assault at Lewes Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction on count 3 held not necessarily inconsistent with acquittals on other counts.
enrichment.ratio: A jury may convict on one sexual offence count while acquitting on others where each allegation is considered separately; credibility and reliability are not indivisible, and appellate intervention requires demonstration that no reasonable jury could rationally reach the mixed verdicts.
legal_issues: Whether conviction on one count was inconsistent with acquittals on related counts
Application of R v G principles to sexual offence trials
Whether jury could be sure of the first incident but not later allegations
Standard for impugning verdicts as inconsistent
linked_authorities: R v G [1998] Crim LR 483
Cilgram [1994] Crim CR 861

confidence.notes: Legal principles and application to mixed verdicts are clearly stated. No complaint was made about the summing-up.

notes: Kastor Too marine insurance; constructive total loss by fire upheld though sinking from separate cause; costs cross-appeal allowed.

enrichment.short_title: Kastor Too: constructive total loss and marine insurance costs
key_facts: The bulk carrier Kastor Too suffered an engine-room fire on 9 March 2000 and sank the next day in deep water off Yemen while insured for US$3 million.
Tomlinson J held fire caused a constructive total loss but that sinking resulted from independent unexplained ingress of seawater, rejecting the actual total loss claim.
Owners amended to claim constructive total loss when repair costs before sinking exceeded agreed value; insurers appealed on abandonment and merger principles.
A 17-day trial involved extensive expert evidence; owners bettered a Part 36 offer but the judge ordered them to pay 70% of insurers' costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from Commercial Court judgment on marine insurance total loss and costs.
enrichment.outcome: Insurers' appeal on constructive total loss dismissed; cross-appeal on costs allowed with no order for costs at first instance; insurers ordered to pay 70% of owners' appeal costs.
enrichment.ratio: A constructive total loss by an insured peril may be claimed even when followed by an actual total loss from a separate cause, where notice of abandonment is excused and the merger rule in section 77(2) does not swallow a prior constructive total loss that was not treated as a partial loss.
legal_issues: Whether constructive total loss by fire was overtaken and merged into subsequent sinking
Requirements for notice of abandonment under sections 61 and 62
Causation of sinking versus insurable constructive total loss from fire damage
Appropriate costs order where actual total loss claim failed but constructive total loss succeeded
linked_authorities: Pesquerias y Descongelados SA v Beer [1946] 79 Ll L Rep 417
Kaltenbach v Mackenzie (1878) 3 CPD 467
Rankin v Potter (1873) LR 8 CP 105
British & Foreign Insurance Co v Wilson Shipping Co [1921] 1 AC 188
Royal Boskalis Westminster NV v Mountain [1999] QB 674

confidence.notes: Very long judgment but CLT outcome, merger analysis and costs decision are clearly stated in the order and reasoning.

notes: MHRT absolute discharge without Home Office notice; natural justice breach requires quashing and rehearing.

enrichment.short_title: MHRT absolute discharge without Secretary of State notice
key_facts: The interested party was convicted of arson endangering life and made subject to section 37 hospital and section 41 restriction orders without limit of time.
She received a deferred conditional discharge in March 2002 and an absolute discharge from the Mental Health Review Tribunal in September 2003.
The Secretary of State was not notified of the application and could not submit his mandatory views on suitability for absolute discharge.
The Tribunal conceded breach of the Rules and natural justice; the patient opposed quashing despite sympathy for her position.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review by the Secretary of State against MHRT decision to grant absolute discharge to a conditionally discharged restricted patient.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed; matter remitted to a differently constituted Mental Health Review Tribunal for rehearing de novo.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to notify the Secretary of State of a restricted patient's application for absolute discharge is a fundamental breach of natural justice and undermines the statutory scheme by which the Secretary of State alone represents the public interest in recall and discharge decisions.
legal_issues: Whether failure to notify the Secretary of State vitiated the Tribunal's absolute discharge decision
Whether the court should exercise discretion not to quash despite procedural breach
Role of the Secretary of State under Rule 6(3) for conditionally discharged patients
Whether participation would have made no difference to the outcome
index_terms: R v Oxford Regional MHRT ex p Home Secretary
linked_authorities: R v Oxford Regional Mental Health Review Tribunal, Ex p Secretary of State for the Home Department [1988] AC 120
Main v Swansea City Council and Others [1985] 45 P & CR 26
